name: Haroi
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, primary stress on the main = final syllable, final stress with the first of two presyllables slightly heavier) rests on the dedicated Haroi phonemic description (Mundhenk & Goschnick 1977, PL A-48), which is the best description of Haroi word prosody that exists per Glottolog's bibliography; no grammar, later phonology, or instrumental study of Haroi is listed or was found in open repositories. The source was not yet obtained before; it is now downloaded and the quotation is confirmed verbatim on p.13. Only housekeeping: the locator should read 'sec. 5 Stress, p.13' (not 'sec.6'), and the grade field is empty and can be filled now that the primary source is held and verified. Lee 1977 and Goschnick 1977 (same volume) were read and are silent on stress, so nothing contradicts the record.

sources.citation: Tegenfeldt Mundhenk & Goschnick 1977, Haroi Phonemes, Pacific Linguistics A-48, sec.6 Stress (full PDF read via sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/)
sources.quote: In Haroi the main syllable is stressed and the presyllable is unstressed. In the case of two presyllables, the first is slightly heavier stressed than the second presyllable.

sources.citation: Mundhenk, Alice Tegenfeldt & Hella Goschnick. 1977. Haroi Phonemes. In D. Thomas, E. W. Lee & Nguyen Dang Liem (eds.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 4: Chamic Studies, 1-16. Pacific Linguistics A-48. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A48.1
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In Haroi the main syllable is stressed and the presyllable is unstressed. In the case of two presyllables, the first is slightly heavier stressed than the second presyllable.' (p.13); 'Haroi words are made up of a main syllable which may be preceded by one or two unstressed presyllables.' (p.9)
